title: Respiratory Medications & Inhaler Safety: Relievers, Controllers, Technique and Deterioration
html:
Respiratory medications can relax airway smooth muscle, reduce inflammation, alter secretions, or modify immune pathways, but the prescription works only when the correct drug reaches the lungs through correct technique. The RN must distinguish rapid symptom relief from long-term control, assess whether worsening symptoms reflect poor technique, under-treatment, overuse, toxicity, infection, or a life-threatening exacerbation, and evaluate the client—not just the inhaler count.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate reliever and controller therapies.
  • Compare beta2 agonists, antimuscarinics, corticosteroids, leukotriene modifiers, methylxanthines, and biologics.
  • Teach and validate metered-dose, dry-powder, soft-mist, spacer, and nebulizer technique.
  • Recognize paradoxical bronchospasm, excessive beta agonist effects, steroid complications, and theophylline toxicity.
  • Use symptom, function, rescue-use, peak-flow, oxygenation, and exacerbation trends to evaluate control.
  • Escalate promptly when medication is not relieving respiratory distress.

Reliever and controller are clinical roles

A reliever is used according to the prescribed action plan for rapid relief of bronchoconstriction. A controller reduces future symptoms and exacerbation risk through regular anti-inflammatory or long-acting therapy. Some inhaled corticosteroid–formoterol regimens serve both roles; therefore, identify the exact product and written plan rather than assuming every combination inhaler is used the same way.

Frequent reliever use, nighttime symptoms, activity limitation, falling peak flow, repeated exacerbations, or failure to obtain relief can signal poor control. Do not simply encourage more unscheduled doses without assessing severity, adherence, inhaler technique, triggers, and the action plan.

Assess respiratory status before and after treatment

Assess respiratory rate, depth and pattern, work of breathing, ability to speak, mental status, breath sounds and air movement, cough and secretions, oxygen saturation in context, prescribed oxygen, heart rate and rhythm, symptom onset, trigger exposure, recent medications, and the client's personal best peak flow when used.

Severe retractions, silent or markedly diminished air entry, cyanosis, exhaustion, altered consciousness, inability to speak, worsening hypercapnia, or poor response to rescue therapy indicates a respiratory emergency. A decreasing respiratory rate is not reassuring when the client is tiring.

A quiet chest can be dangerous
Less wheezing with worsening distress may mean critically reduced airflow, not improvement. Reassess air movement, effort, speech, mentation, oxygenation and response, and activate emergency care.

Short-acting beta2 agonists provide rapid bronchodilation

Albuterol and related short-acting beta2 agonists relax bronchial smooth muscle. Monitor respiratory response, heart rate, tremor, palpitations, chest discomfort, potassium when intensive repeated therapy makes it relevant, and the frequency of use. Excess exposure can contribute to tachycardia, dysrhythmia, tremor, hyperglycemia, and hypokalemia.

A SABA is not a substitute for appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment in asthma. If repeated prescribed doses do not improve airflow and distress, escalate; continued self-administration can delay definitive treatment. Paradoxical bronchospasm—sudden worsening immediately after inhalation—requires stopping the product and urgent assessment.

Long-acting beta agonists require diagnosis-specific use

Long-acting beta agonists maintain bronchodilation but are not all suitable for immediate rescue. In asthma, a LABA should be used in an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing regimen; LABA monotherapy does not address airway inflammation. Formoterol has a rapid onset and may serve as reliever only in a specifically prescribed corticosteroid-containing regimen.

Verify the product, device, frequency, and role. Duplicate LABA exposure can occur when multiple combination inhalers are prescribed or reconciled incorrectly.

Antimuscarinics reduce cholinergic bronchoconstriction

Ipratropium is short acting; tiotropium and other long-acting muscarinic antagonists provide maintenance bronchodilation. They are important in COPD and may be added in selected asthma plans. Monitor breathing, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, and precipitation of narrow-angle glaucoma symptoms if aerosol enters the eyes.

Antimuscarinics are not interchangeable by device or schedule. Teach correct device preparation and avoid spraying mist into the eyes. Assess urinary obstruction risk and the client's ability to generate the required inspiratory flow.

Inhaled corticosteroids control inflammation

Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation and exacerbation risk but do not provide instant relief of acute bronchospasm. Teach regular use as prescribed, correct technique, and mouth rinsing and spitting after administration to reduce oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia. A spacer or valved holding chamber with a compatible metered-dose inhaler can improve delivery and reduce mouth deposition.

Inspect for thrush, hoarseness, technique problems, and adherence barriers. At higher or prolonged exposures, consider systemic effects such as adrenal suppression, bone and eye effects, skin bruising, and growth effects in children according to the treatment plan. Use the prescribed lowest effective regimen; do not stop abruptly without review.

Systemic corticosteroids require broad surveillance

Oral or IV corticosteroids may be used for moderate or severe exacerbations and other pulmonary inflammation. Monitor glucose, blood pressure, fluid balance, mood and sleep, infection, gastrointestinal risk, wound healing, and electrolyte effects. Longer therapy can suppress the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, so abrupt discontinuation may be unsafe.

Corticosteroids can mask infection signs. Improvement in wheeze does not eliminate the need to evaluate fever, sputum change, hemodynamics, and the overall clinical course.

Leukotriene modifiers and montelukast warning

Montelukast is a controller, not a rescue bronchodilator. The FDA boxed warning describes serious neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts or actions. Assess behavioral and mental-health history, teach clients and caregivers to watch for sleep, mood, behavior, or thinking changes, and follow the current plan for stopping and contacting the prescriber if these occur.

For allergic rhinitis, montelukast use is generally reserved for clients who do not respond to or tolerate alternatives. Continue monitoring even without prior psychiatric illness because events have occurred in clients with and without such history.

Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range

Theophylline provides bronchodilation but has a narrow safety margin and many drug, smoking, illness, and dietary interactions. Clearance may change with fever, liver disease, heart failure, age, tobacco exposure, and newly started or stopped medications.

Early toxicity may cause nausea, vomiting, insomnia, headache, or tremor; serious toxicity can cause persistent tachycardia, dysrhythmias, hypotension, or seizures. Verify serum-level timing, dose history, interactions, and symptoms. Hold and escalate according to the current order or protocol rather than relying on an isolated level.

Mucolytics, expectorants and cough medications

Mucoactive therapy is most effective when matched to secretion characteristics, hydration status, airway clearance ability, and diagnosis. Nebulized acetylcysteine can provoke bronchospasm and requires preparedness for airway response. Expectorants do not replace hydration or airway clearance when those are appropriate.

Cough can protect the airway. Antitussives require assessment of cause, respiratory drive, sedation risk, secretion retention, and interactions. Opioid-containing cough products can depress respirations and should not be treated as harmless over-the-counter therapy.

Biologics require phenotype and reaction monitoring

Biologic agents target specific allergic or eosinophilic pathways in selected severe asthma. They are add-on controller therapy, not rescue treatment. Verify dose, interval, indication, prior response, infection or vaccine considerations specific to the product, and observation requirements.

Hypersensitivity, including delayed reactions, can occur. Ensure required emergency resources and teach clients to seek help for breathing difficulty, swelling, hives, dizziness, or systemic symptoms after administration.

Device technique determines delivered dose

Identify the exact device because steps differ. For a pressurized metered-dose inhaler, common steps include removing the cap, checking and priming when required, shaking suspensions, exhaling away from the device, sealing lips, beginning a slow deep inhalation while actuating once, continuing to inhale, holding the breath when able, and waiting as directed before another puff. A compatible spacer reduces coordination demands.

A dry-powder inhaler generally requires a forceful deep inhalation and should not be shaken or exhaled into because moisture can damage the powder. A soft-mist inhaler has its own loading and slow-inhalation sequence. Nebulizers require correct medication, assembly, interface, flow source, cleaning, and infection-control practices.

Ask the client to demonstrate with their own device. Teach-back should verify preparation, breathing pattern, dose counter, cleaning, storage, and how to know when the device is empty. A canister may still spray propellant after active medication is depleted.

Sequence multiple inhaled medicines intentionally

When bronchodilator and inhaled corticosteroid doses are both prescribed, bronchodilation is commonly given first when the plan specifies it, followed by the anti-inflammatory inhaler; exact sequence and interval depend on products and orders. Rinse and spit after the corticosteroid. Do not combine nebulizer solutions unless compatibility and the prescription are verified.

Asthma and COPD plans are not interchangeable

Asthma treatment prioritizes anti-inflammatory therapy because variable airway inflammation drives risk. COPD treatment emphasizes long-acting bronchodilation, with inhaled corticosteroids added for selected exacerbation and eosinophil patterns while considering pneumonia risk. A medication appropriate for one diagnosis may have a different role in the other.

Smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation, trigger reduction, and written action plans complement medication therapy. Oxygen is a prescribed treatment and should be titrated to the client-specific target; do not withhold needed oxygen from a hypoxemic client based on a myth about respiratory drive.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify diagnosis, symptom pattern, work of breathing, air movement, oxygenation, reliever frequency, action-plan zone, peak flow, product, device, technique, adherence, interactions, and adverse effects.
  2. Analyze cues: Determine whether symptoms reflect bronchospasm, inflammation, secretion burden, infection, poor delivery, overuse, medication toxicity, or respiratory fatigue.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Impending respiratory failure, anaphylaxis, paradoxical bronchospasm, severe dysrhythmia, seizure, and suicidal thinking require urgent response.
  4. Generate solutions: Support ventilation and oxygenation, follow the action plan, correct technique, reconcile duplicate ingredients, prepare rescue treatment, and escalate therapy review.
  5. Take action: Administer the correct product by the correct device, stop harmful exposure, activate emergency care when needed, and use demonstration-based teaching.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess effort, speech, air movement, respiratory rate, oxygenation, heart rate, symptoms, function, rescue-use frequency, peak flow, adverse effects, and return precautions.

Clinical example

A client with asthma has used an albuterol inhaler repeatedly but is now speaking one word at a time, becoming drowsy, and has barely audible breath sounds. The RN does not interpret reduced wheezing as improvement. The RN activates emergency response, supports airway, breathing and prescribed oxygenation, administers emergency medications according to protocol, applies continuous monitoring, and prepares for advanced ventilatory support. After stabilization, the team reviews controller use, inhaler technique, triggers, and the written action plan.

Respiratory medication selection, device technique, action plans, oxygen targets, monitoring, and emergency treatment require current prescriptions, product instructions, client-specific assessment, organizational protocols, respiratory and pharmacy resources, and qualified clinical supervision.
